children.text: As discussed in the previous page, how we categorize the world tells us as much about our own categorical systems as it does about the world itself. Among the species that share this planet with us, ocean mammals have been particularly associated with “playfulness.” Play, in this sense, is one of the many ways cetaceans especially come to be read as “more-like-us”, compared to other species.

When we look for animals that seem like us, two groups keep surfacing: primates and cetaceans. Primates hold that likeness through evolutionary genealogy. Chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest living relatives, sharing a common ancestor with humans roughly six to seven million years ago and some 98–99% of our DNA. Cetaceans hold it differently, through behaviour and affect rather than ancestry: they are known for being emotionally intelligent, highly social creatures who form tight family units and durable bonds, and who seem, watching them, to be having something like fun.

Dolphins, for example, are known for their playful antics. They demonstrate many traits of play, from acrobatics to games with objects. Similarly, other marine animals, like seals and otters, engage in playful behaviours. These activities serve various purposes, from honing skills to social bonding. Animal behaviourists explores play in marine animals to understand their cognitive abilities and social dynamics.
